prompt: Match each check to what a "no" makes the platform do.

pairs.right: kill the process and start another
stop sending it traffic, and wait
hold liveness off while a slow start finishes

right_distractors: restore the database from a backup

prompt: The database goes down, and every copy's liveness check pings it. What follows?

choices.text: Traffic moves to the copies whose database connection still works
choices.why: Every copy fails at the same moment; there is no copy that still works.

choices.text: Nothing happens until the database returns
choices.why: A failed liveness check makes the platform kill the process.

choices.text: The database restarts
choices.why: The platform acts on the process whose check failed, not on the database.

choices.text: Every copy is restarted, over and over
choices.why: Right. A restarted boxoffice reaches a dead database no better than the old one, and the restarts add load.

prompt: Why does boxoffice serve its health checks and metrics on `-ops`, never published to the internet?

choices.text: Prometheus refuses to scrape a port that serves anything else
choices.why: Prometheus scrapes any URL it is given.

choices.text: Go's `http.Server` allows only one handler function on each port it listens on
choices.why: The main port serves dozens of routes.

choices.text: They serve the machinery, and expose the service's insides
choices.why: Right. The platform reaches the port from inside the network; customers never need it.

choices.text: HTTP/2 needs a port of its own
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson is about HTTP/2.

prompt: Why does boxoffice have no startup probe?
hint: What is a startup probe for?

choices.text: Docker ignores startup probes
choices.why: The reason is boxoffice's start time, not Docker.

choices.text: Startup probes test the database, which liveness must never do
choices.why: A startup probe holds liveness off; it tests nothing in particular.

choices.text: Readiness already restarts a slow process
choices.why: Readiness never restarts anything; it withholds traffic.

choices.text: boxoffice starts in milliseconds, so nothing needs holding off
choices.why: Right. The probe exists for processes that take minutes, so liveness does not kill them meanwhile.

prompt: Why does `ready` give its database ping a one-second limit?
hint: The platform asks every few seconds.

choices.text: A late answer is useless, and calls pile up
choices.why: Right. A slow check is a useless one, and the next call arrives before the last one ends.

choices.text: pgx refuses longer pings
choices.why: The limit is boxoffice's choice, passed in a context.

choices.text: One second is the Kubernetes default probe timeout
choices.why: The lesson gives its reason as the readiness check itself, not a Kubernetes default.

choices.text: The pool lesson 9 configured closes any connection that has been idle for a second
choices.why: Lesson 9 set five minutes for idle connections.

prompt: PostgreSQL was stopped under the running server. Match each request to its answer.
After PostgreSQL came back, `/readyz` said `ready`. What was still broken?
hint: The first line of the grep.

choices.text: The pool, which never reconnects
choices.why: The pool opened new connections by itself; `/readyz` and requests worked.

choices.text: The migrations, which had to run again
choices.why: Stopping a server keeps its data and schema.

choices.text: Every live page: `listen` had returned and nothing started it again
choices.why: Right. Readiness checked the database, not the listener, so frozen pages passed as ready.

choices.text: `/healthz`, which kept answering 503
choices.why: `/healthz` answered 200 throughout.

prompt: What does section 03 give as the fix for the frozen live pages?

choices.text: Restart boxoffice every time the database restarts
choices.why: That is the restart loop again, done by hand.

choices.text: Reconnect `listen` in a loop; make readiness cover it
choices.why: Right. Lesson 13 named the loop; readiness then says so when live updates are dead.

choices.text: Check the database in `/healthz` as well
choices.why: That is section 02's trap, and the database was already back.

choices.text: Poll the database every second from each page, and drop notifications altogether
choices.why: That replaces notifications with polling and leaves the dead listener in place.

prompt: Why does `/healthz` include the version?

choices.text: It says which build runs where
choices.why: Right. It is the first question anybody asks during a deploy.

choices.text: Kubernetes compares it with the image tag
choices.why: Kubernetes reads only the status code of an HTTP probe.

choices.text: Without a body, a 200 counts as a failure
choices.why: An HTTP probe judges the status code alone.

choices.text: It proves the database schema matches
choices.why: `live` touches nothing outside the process.

prompt: Match each kind of metric to boxoffice's example of it.
Why are the two gauges `GaugeFunc`s?

choices.text: Prometheus accepts no other kind of gauge
choices.why: client_golang has ordinary gauges set by `Set`, `Inc` and `Dec`.

choices.text: Functions are cheaper to label than gauges that are set by hand
choices.why: These two gauges carry no labels at all.

choices.text: They read the hub and the pool at the moment of each scrape, never stale
choices.why: Right. Nothing has to remember to update them.

choices.text: They reset to zero after each scrape
choices.why: No metric resets on a scrape.

prompt: Why does `metricsHandler` use a registry of its own?
hint: Instead of the library's global one.

choices.text: The global registry is not safe for concurrent use
choices.why: The reason is what ends up on the page, not concurrency.

choices.text: The global one serves only JSON
choices.why: Both serve the same text format.

choices.text: Prometheus scrapes only registries created per handler
choices.why: Prometheus reads a URL; it knows nothing of registries.

choices.text: To serve only what boxoffice registers
choices.why: Right. Only what boxoffice registers is served.

prompt: Why does `measure` label requests with `r.Pattern` and never with the path?
hint: Each label value is a time series.

choices.text: Paths carry the request id, which must stay out of every metric
choices.why: The request id travels in a header, not in the path.

choices.text: Prometheus forbids slashes in labels
choices.why: The pattern has slashes too.

choices.text: The path is empty after `requireStaff`
choices.why: The path is always there.

choices.text: A path makes unbounded series
choices.why: Right. Patterns are a number you wrote; paths are whatever arrives.

prompt: Why must `measure` be the last middleware in the chain, next to the mux?
hint: Who writes the pattern, and into what?

choices.text: The mux writes the pattern into its own request
choices.why: Right. Next to the mux, `measure` hands over its own request and reads the pattern afterwards.

choices.text: It must run after `cors` has answered preflights
choices.why: Order with `cors` is not the reason; the pattern is.

choices.text: Otherwise it counts each request twice
choices.why: It runs once per request wherever it sits.

choices.text: The status recorder works only next to the mux
choices.why: `logRequests` uses the same recorder at the outside of the chain.

prompt: Which route label does `GET /admin/report` get?

choices.text: `GET /admin/report`
choices.why: That pattern is written into a copy `measure` never sees.

choices.text: `unmatched`
choices.why: The outer mux matched it, so it has a pattern.

choices.text: the path, `/admin/report`
choices.why: `measure` never labels by path.

choices.text: `/admin/`
choices.why: Right. The outer pattern; the inner mux writes into a copy.

prompt: Under which route was the 404 for `/events/9` counted?

choices.text: `GET /events/{id}`
choices.why: Right. The handler said the event does not exist.

choices.text: `unmatched`
choices.why: That was `/nowhere`, which no route matched.

choices.text: None: errors are not counted
choices.why: Every status is counted, a 500 included.

choices.text: `GET /events`
choices.why: That pattern lists events and takes no id.

prompt: Match each letter of RED to what it asks.
right_distractors: how much memory the process holds

prompt: A hundred requests take 2 ms and one takes 4 seconds. What is the mean, in milliseconds, rounded to a whole number?
What does a histogram keep that the mean of the same requests hides?

choices.text: The request ids of the slow ones
choices.why: Request ids never go in a label; they belong in the log.

choices.text: The exact duration of each request
choices.why: Buckets count observations up to a bound; the exact values are gone.

choices.text: The shape: many fast requests and one slow one
choices.why: Right. A 42 ms mean describes none of them; the buckets show both.

choices.text: The client that sent each request
choices.why: Nothing about the client is in the metric.

prompt: Which of these belongs in a metric's label?
hint: A small set known in advance.

choices.text: the HTTP status
choices.why: Right. A few dozen values at most, all known.

choices.text: the customer's e-mail address
choices.why: Unbounded, and personal data copied into a system kept for months.

choices.text: the request id
choices.why: Unbounded; it belongs in the log.

choices.text: the ticket id
choices.why: One value per sale, without bound.

prompt: Why do the live streams not drag up the purchase route's latency?
hint: They land in the top buckets.

choices.text: `measure` skips requests longer than 30 seconds
choices.why: Longer ones are counted in `+Inf`.

choices.text: Hijacked requests never reach `measure`
choices.why: The server-sent event stream is not hijacked, and it is measured.

choices.text: Prometheus drops observations above the last bucket
choices.why: They go into `+Inf`; nothing is dropped.

choices.text: Streams are counted under their own route label
choices.why: Right. Each route is its own histogram.

prompt: `/metrics` answered 158 lines. What would tens of thousands mean?

choices.text: The Go runtime is leaking goroutines
choices.why: A goroutine leak raises one number, not the line count.

choices.text: A label has escaped into unbounded values
choices.why: Right. A few thousand is normal for a large service.

choices.text: Prometheus has not scraped for a while
choices.why: The page shows current values; scrapes do not add lines.

choices.text: Many more requests arrived than in the transcript, raising every counter on the page
choices.why: More requests raise counters, not the number of series.

prompt: Order what boxoffice does after the first `SIGTERM`.
items: `srv.Shutdown` closes the listeners and waits for active requests
`GracefulStop` waits for gRPC calls, until the deadline
stop the ops server and return from `main`

prompt: Why did the hub get a `done` channel, closed through `RegisterOnShutdown`?

choices.text: `Shutdown` closes every channel in the program
choices.why: `Shutdown` knows nothing of channels.

choices.text: Streams never end on their own, and hijacked WebSockets are not tracked
choices.why: Right. Without it, streams hold the shutdown to its deadline and WebSockets are dropped.

choices.text: PostgreSQL stops sending notifications on `SIGTERM`
choices.why: The signal goes to boxoffice, not to the database.

choices.text: To count the open streams for section 04's `boxoffice_live_watchers` gauge
choices.why: `count` does that; `done` ends the streams.

prompt: Why does `hub.close` use `sync.Once`?
hint: What does closing a closed channel do?

choices.text: It makes `close` faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: `RegisterOnShutdown` calls every function three times
choices.why: It calls each registered function once per `Shutdown`.

choices.text: Closing a closed channel panics
choices.why: Right. `Once` makes a second call harmless.

choices.text: Go forbids closing a channel without a lock
choices.why: Closing a channel needs no lock.

prompt: Which WebSocket close status does boxoffice send when it shuts down?
In section 06's run, what did the slow purchase get?
hint: It was in flight when the signal arrived.

choices.text: A connection reset by the server at the moment of the signal
choices.why: That is lesson 16's behaviour, before the graceful shutdown.

choices.text: A 503, because readiness had turned
choices.why: Readiness answers the platform; the request already in flight went on.

choices.text: 201, after 2.2 seconds, a second after the signal
choices.why: Right. The process logged `stopped` and exited with 0 only after it.

choices.text: A 500, because the signal cancelled its transaction halfway
choices.why: Nothing cancelled it; `Shutdown` waited for it.

prompt: Why is the shutdown timeout eight seconds by default?

choices.text: Prometheus scrapes every eight seconds
choices.why: The scrape interval has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: gRPC refuses longer deadlines
choices.why: The deadline is boxoffice's own context.

choices.text: Eight seconds is the longest a purchase was measured to take in lesson 9's tests
choices.why: No such measurement was made.

choices.text: It must end before the platform's `SIGKILL`
choices.why: Right. boxoffice cuts the stragglers itself, cleanly, first.

prompt: In the server's terminal, what did `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` report?

choices.text: `cut`'s exit status
choices.why: That is `$?` after a pipeline.

choices.text: the number of lines `cut` shortened
choices.why: `PIPESTATUS` holds exit statuses.

choices.text: the signal number of `SIGTERM`
choices.why: It printed `exit 0`.

choices.text: boxoffice's exit status, 0
choices.why: Right. The first command of the pipeline.

prompt: Why does `main` call `stop` right after the signal context ends?

choices.text: To close the database pool
choices.why: The deferred `pool.Close` does that when `main` returns.

choices.text: To start the shutdown timer
choices.why: `context.WithTimeout` starts it.

choices.text: To send `SIGTERM` to the gRPC server
choices.why: The gRPC server runs in the same process.

choices.text: So a second signal kills it
choices.why: Right. Pressing Ctrl-C twice means exactly that.

prompt: Why does `GracefulStop` run in a goroutine, with `Stop` after the deadline?

choices.text: `GracefulStop` returns an error that must be read in parallel
choices.why: It returns nothing.

choices.text: `Watch` streams never end, so `GracefulStop` alone would wait forever
choices.why: Right. `Stop` cuts them when the deadline passes.

choices.text: `Stop` drains calls more gently
choices.why: `Stop` cuts calls; `GracefulStop` is the gentle one.

choices.text: gRPC must stop before HTTP
choices.why: HTTP's `Shutdown` runs first.

prompt: When `Shutdown` is called, `ListenAndServe` returns `http.___`, which `main` treats as expected rather than fatal.
Match each value in section 07's Kubernetes snippet to what it sets.

pairs.right: three failures in a row before a restart

prompt: Which statements match this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The image sets `BOXOFFICE_OPS=:9100` so the ops port listens on every interface
choices.why: Right. Inside a container, `localhost` is the container itself.

choices.text: Liveness pings the database with a one-second limit
choices.why: That is readiness; liveness touches nothing outside the process.

choices.text: The PromQL in section 05 was run against a Prometheus server
choices.why: The course installed no Prometheus; the expressions were not run.

choices.text: boxoffice keeps no delay between readiness turning 503 and `Shutdown`
choices.why: Right. On a platform that needs one, that delay is one more setting.

choices.text: The stream in section 06 ended with curl's status 0
choices.why: Right. The server closed the response properly.

prompt: Kubernetes removes a stopping pod from the load balancer and signals it at about the same moment. What follows for boxoffice as written?

choices.text: Nothing: readiness turns 503 before any request arrives
choices.why: Readiness is asked every few seconds; the removal lags behind the signal.

choices.text: Kubernetes waits for `/readyz` to answer 503 before signalling
choices.why: It signals without asking.

choices.text: For a second or two, requests keep arriving at a listener that is already closed
choices.why: Right. Serving a few more seconds after readiness turns 503 is the common answer.

choices.text: The pod restarts, because liveness fails
choices.why: `/healthz` keeps answering 200 during the shutdown.
